title: Days, dates, and daily routines
title_target: วันนี้วันอะไร — Wan-níi wan à-rai
goal: Name days and dates, describe your daily routine from waking up to going to bed, and use time adverbs — all without changing a single verb form.

say dates and understand the Buddhist year
describe your daily activities in order

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — Coffee break, talking about the weekend
dialogs.intro: Nok asks about Budi's habits. Notice one thing that should be a relief: not a single verb in this dialogue changes form, whether for yesterday, today, or tomorrow.

notes: **Day names always start with วัน wan (day).** *วันจันทร์* (Monday), *วันอังคาร* (Tuesday), and so on. In fast speech *วัน* is often dropped: *เสาร์อาทิตย์นี้* = this weekend.

**The seven day names come from the planets, just as English Sunday, Monday, and Saturday do** — here via Sanskrit: *อาทิตย์ aa-thít* (Sunday/the sun) is related to Sanskrit "Aditya", *จันทร์ jan* (Monday/the moon) to "Chandra", *ศุกร์ sùk* (Friday/Venus) to "Shukra". Sun-day and Moon-day work the same way in both languages.

**Each day has its own color in Thailand**, and it's more than an old belief: Monday's color is yellow, and to this day many people wear yellow on Mondays. The colors: Sunday red, Monday yellow, Tuesday pink, Wednesday green, Thursday orange, Friday blue, Saturday purple.
**Dates use วันที่ wan-thîi + number.** *วันที่สิบห้า* = the 15th. The full order: *วันที่ 15 เดือนธันวาคม ปี 2569* — day, month, year, as in British English.

**Thailand's official year is the Buddhist Era, 543 years ahead of the Western calendar.** 2026 = 2569 พ.ศ. This number turns up on receipts, ID cards, and expiry dates. If you see "2569", don't panic — subtract 543.

**Month names have an ending that tells you the number of days**, and that's the key to learning them: 31-day months end in **-คม *-khom***, 30-day months end in **-ยน *-yon***, and February stands alone with **-พันธ์ *-phan***. So *มกราคม* must have 31 days, *เมษายน* must have 30.
**เคย khoei means "have ever" and goes before the verb.** *เคยไป* (have been), *ไม่เคยกิน* (have never eaten). Short answers: *เคยครับ* (yes, I have) or *ไม่เคยครับ* (no, never).

**หน้า nâa means "front", and with time it means "next".** *เดือนหน้า* (next month), *อาทิตย์หน้า* (next week), *ปีหน้า* (next year). The opposite is *ที่แล้ว thîi-láaeo*: *เดือนที่แล้ว* (last month).

blocks.title: Three linking words that make your story flow
items: **แล้วก็ *láaeo kâw*** — "and then". *อาบน้ำแล้วก็กินข้าว* = shower and then eat.
**ก่อน *kàwn*** — "first, beforehand", placed **at the end**: *กินข้าวก่อน* = eat first.
**หลังจากนั้น *lǎng-jàak-nán*** — "after that". A little more formal, good for storytelling.

blocks.text: A complete example: *ปกติผมตื่นหกโมงครึ่ง อาบน้ำแล้วก็กินข้าวเช้า แปดโมงไปทำงาน เลิกงานหกโมงเย็น กลับบ้านแล้วก็ทำอาหาร นอนประมาณห้าทุ่มครับ* — and that's your whole workday in one breath.
The Thai calendar has many holidays, and some of them transform the whole country. Knowing them saves you from closed offices and sold-out tickets.

blocks.title: สงกรานต์ and one thing to prepare for
items: During Songkran, **every street turns into a water fight** for three full days — with no exceptions for people in a hurry or in nice clothes. Keep your phone in a plastic bag.
The tradition's roots are gentle: pouring scented water over elders' hands as a sign of respect and a request for blessings. The water fight is the rowdy version.
A useful phrase: **สวัสดีปีใหม่ไทย *sà-wàt-dii pii-mài thai*** — happy Thai New Year. Said while soaking wet, it always gets a laugh.
